The story telling and atmosphere are among the best I have ever experienced. Do yourself a favor and don't look anything up for your first go. Take your time and explore. Find the story. I am frugal, and I am so glad I took the time and spend the money for a great experience. The great graphics and physics definitely help the experience. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

As someone who’s been playing these types of games for years, I was excited to finally try SOMA, given its reputation as one of the greats. But after finishing it, I can’t help but feel it’s overhyped and underwhelming. It’s not even that the game is outright bad; it’s just painfully mediocre in almost every aspect, and I’ve seen it all done better elsewhere.

Let’s start with the story, which is supposed to be SOMA’s strongest point. Frankly, The narrative about artificial intelligence, human consciousness, and what it means to exist has been recycled in countless books, movies, and games. It doesn’t offer a fresh perspective or compelling twists, and the delivery is heavy-handed. You can practically feel the game yelling, “Look how deep we are!” without giving you anything new to chew on. The story lacks emotional impact because it never really surprises or challenges you. If you’ve played or watched anything in the sci-fi genre, you’ve probably seen this exact plot before.

The gameplay doesn’t do the story any favors, either. The stealth mechanics are clunky, repetitive, and downright frustrating. The enemies aren’t scary or intimidating—they’re just an obstacle you have to slowly tiptoe around. These moments are meant to build tension, but they end up feeling more like a waste of time. Instead of enhancing the horror, they drag the whole experience down.

Then there’s the pacing, which is all over the place. The game grinds to a halt with tedious "puzzles", backtracking, and slow, drawn-out dialogue that overstays its welcome. Any tension the game manages to create is quickly squashed by these pacing issues. While the atmosphere is decent in parts, it’s not enough to keep you engaged when the gameplay and story fail to deliver.

The most disappointing thing is how overhyped SOMA is. People talk about it like it’s a masterpiece, but in reality, it’s a shallow, recycled narrative wrapped in uninspired gameplay. The only reason I stuck with it was to get all the achievements - because by the halfway point, I wasn’t playing for enjoyment anymore.

If you’re new to the genre, you might find SOMA somewhat enjoyable. However, I found it to be a lackluster and forgettable experience. It’s far from the groundbreaking, thought-provoking game it’s often made out to be - just another recycled sci-fi story that leaves no lasting impression.

[h2]Psychosoma, [i]qu’est-ce que c’est[/i]?[/h2]

[i]Amnesia: The Dark Descent[/i] made sure no talk of video game horror could go along without the mention of Frictional Games—the terrible, downright evil studio that not only dared deliver yet another horror game that completely lacked combat, but one that was so good and infectious that its stylings shaped the genre for almost a decade.

While we’ll probably never glimpse the terrible truth and come to an agreement on whether horror needs to opt out of combat entirely to be scary, Frictional’s follow-up title, [i]SOMA[/i], made a compelling argument that its exclusion is sometimes the only way of having your message heard. Unobscured by the whirls of revved-up chainsaws and the flashes of plasma cutters, it can still shine down there, in the quiet and the dark.

For [i]SOMA[/i], however, it’s not just important to hear what it has to say, but also how it says it. For a true barotraumatic dive into its thematic depths, take a look at the full version of [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/drugoja/recommended/282140/]this[/url] review, written by the ever-curious [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/40848670-Drugoja-In-The-Dreaming/]Drugoja in the Dreaming[/url]. Be warned that it will spoil all there is to spoil, so stick with me if you’ve yet to play the game.

[h3]Love the Body[/h3]

“Play one Frictional title, and you’ve played them all!” would probably be the adage, if not for [i]SOMA[/i]. As far as mechanical complexity is concerned, it’s as stripped back as Frictional’s ever been, serving as a natural progression and iteration of the team’s formula: take away more and more of the player's ability to outright remove the frights in their path and force them to deal with them without using force. In theory, this creates a feeling of helplessness not found in traditional survival horror and primes the player to engage with what’s on the screen in a different, less rigid, mechanically-minded way. The world becomes this real, unfamiliar place, where interactivity isn’t geared towards stuffing your backpack or blasting away at limbs and heads. Yet, remove one challenge of game development by taking an entirely different approach, and another will present itself—and if there’s something that Frictional didn’t learn from [i]The Dark Descent[/i], then they for sure had a cautionary tale in [i]A Machine for Pigs[/i].

For one, [i]The Dark Descent[/i] still had enough resource management to be viewed as nothing more than a clockwork interaction between its mechanics if you were so inclined. It never explicitly got in the way of you tracing back up from and down again into Daniel’s insanity spiral, but the game stopped short of blending the two together. There were glimpses of it, but the need for health bars, depletable light sources, and meters to manage prevailed in the end—this is a video game, after all, a [b]survival[/b] horror one, but something tells me Frictional wanted players to look a bit more beyond that.

The Chinese Room realised this and rid their sequel of tinderboxes and laudanum bottles, but instead of having the player use this newly freed-up attention on something important, they thought a separate window with a thesaurus would do just fine.

To that end, [i]SOMA[/i] is a horror game with puzzle elements, in which you attempt to escape a haywire, underwater facility on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean. Threats lurk about, even if combat is absent. Physical contact between you and these monsters amounts to getting flung across the room and some spooky screen effects should it end fatally. Running, sneaking and puzzling your way out of danger remains the way of getting out of trouble, and an intricate plot backed by heartfelt character drama and eerily genuine voice acting guides you from one setpiece to the next.

It’s a dance Frictional knows well; one that [i]SOMA[/i] comes so close to perfecting, were it not for the obvious criticism that’s been repeated since the very beginning with games of its ilk—it’s not scary. Rather, it’s frustrating and distracts from what’s more important. Any point at which whatever’s chasing you manages to remove those last few bits from your health bar is an almost pointless, immersion-breaking yank that pulls you out of the game. Indeed, an element solely there to make the video game more like a video game is what works against it the most.

It's as if horror games are afraid to entirely remove the fear of death. [i]SOMA[/i] has a Story difficulty, yet it is a band-aid fix to a fundamental design issue. If a tangible threat is what was needed, why not make the very environment something to be afraid of? If the goal was having interactions that are more inspired by the story and setting, rather than the mechanics, why undermine it? I’m sure making the airlock an enemy, by giving it the ability to crush you to a pulp should you miss the warnings on the wall to your left, would have done wonders for making players pay attention and interact with their surroundings in a more natural way. The bottom of the ocean is a scary place, period, no sci-fi monsters needed. Almost as scary as the idea of beefing up the HPL Engine is to Frictional, I’d imagine, to a point where that kind of interactivity would be possible without squinting at blurry textures.

But, even with engine limitations, Frictional’s art and sound direction are exceptional. It is why [i]SOMA’s[/i] rendition of the ocean floor is so inviting to get lost in and explore, even if it’s quite linear and teeters on the edge of falling into the motions of other games like it. But that begs the question: where does [i]SOMA[/i] break the mould?

[h3]Fear the Mind[/h3]

Without having to worry about any kind of resource management, you’re free to direct your attention elsewhere. [i]SOMA’s[/i] monster encounters are a necessary evil with the way the game was designed; they suck, but can’t come close to ruining what’s so great about it. The puzzles are still there, of course, but the menial tasks of rerouting the power to the correct junction or finding the proper keycard can’t compare to the puzzle the game has been built around:

[i]SOMA’s[/i] key themes, the dash of player choice there is, and the very plot are all interwoven with such great care and subtlety that they’d make a seamstress blush. The closer the game got to anything that’d obstruct it, the bigger my lament. In a roundabout way, It goes so far that it makes the lack of combat in [i]The Dark Descent[/i] seem like an oversight—its narrative aspirations were never as grand, so laying even further into traditional survival horror could have had some merit. 

The morality of [i]SOMA[/i] is in the background, ready to creep up on you while your brain works away at the bits it presents. A "throwaway" line, a note on the wall, or an inconspicuous press of some button—it’s all towards a carefully constructed threefold message: whether ominous, hopeful, or just another pondering of whether androids dream of electric sheep, depends on you. No dialogue wheel, no alignment system, or distracting inventories; just you, some annoying monsters, movable boxes, and a choice that informs a different kind of fear.

Sans those annoying monsters, it’s the otherwise thorough departure from survival horror that allows [i]SOMA[/i] to be filled with substance. All the frights—and everything else the game will make you feel—are in its world and the allegory it serves to paint. The psychological horror they’ve been talking about all these years; something a lot of developers have tried. Many may have succeeded, but a lot more missed what the focus should be and the design decisions at play to sharpen it up.

SOMA and the Impossibility of Immortality

This game explores what I consider humanity's most profound preoccupation: the quest for immortality. SOMA presents the two strategies humans have devised to achieve it, revealing them as fundamentally opposed approaches to the same impossible goal.

The first strategy, embodied by the WAU, pursues biological immortality through maintaining singular consciousness. It assumes that bodily continuity equals immortality, that as long as its feedback systems function, the self endures. The WAU's gel preserves biological function at any cost, transforming bodies into grotesque but living vessels.

The second strategy, represented by the ARK, attempts cognitive duplication across different timeframes. It assumes that perfect replication of consciousness equals immortality, that the self can be copied, transferred, and preserved through technological means.

SOMA initially presents both as viable solutions, allowing players to glimpse hope in each approach. But through careful deduction, the game reveals both strategies as fundamentally flawed. Neither the WAU's biological preservation nor the ARK's cognitive duplication addresses the true nature of immortality, which concerns the preservation of self rather than mere feedback systems or copied experiences.

True immortality would require absolute immutability, a complete cessation of change. Yet in a universe where change is the only constant, where the new perpetually displaces the old, such immutability becomes impossible.

If immortality demands immutability, then in a universe of perpetual change, immortality becomes an impossibility.

This is SOMA's ultimate revelation: not that humans have chosen the wrong path to immortality, but that no path exists at all. The game's horror lies not in its monsters or apocalyptic setting, but in this philosophical void, the recognition that our deepest longing is, by definition, unreachable.

It's hard to review horror. Horror is pretty subjective because it relies on making a connection with the viewer. It has to have some strings to pull to be effective. I'm not afraid of spiders. A horror game about spiders isn't going to bother me much, but it could be really effective for someone else. Frictional Games has been making horror games for quite a while, and they've really found a formula that works. They don't focus on the horror. It's not the jump scares of Five Nights at Freddy's. There are no monster closets; you'll know something is coming for you even if you don't know what. No, SOMA focuses on dread. They build a sense of dread, and let the dread invoke horror in the player.

In SOMA, you are Simon Jarrett. You've recently been in a bad car accident that killed your friend and left you brain damage and cranial bleeding. In search of help, you allow someone who's explicitly not a doctor to begin an experimental treatment. He'll make a xerox copy of your brain, treat it until he finds something that works, and then apply that treatment to you. The helmet comes down,the brain copying begins. When the helmet comes off, you're in an derelict underwater station.

This raises a lot of questions, none of which I'll provide as they're half of the point of SOMA. I can assure you that most of the answers are unpleasant. You find them in interactions with the other things at the bottom of the sea. There's also no lack of logs and recordings to find. Like previous Frictional Games, SOMA is about exploration of your surroundings. You'll rummage through drawers, and poke around on the workstations still on. It's a lot of Gone Home (which could be said got a lot of its inspiration from previous Frictional Games) with some hide-and-seek. See, there are also things down there with you that don't want you to survive.

Some have said that the monsters are the worst part of SOMA, but (to me), they're necessary to keeping up the tension. You never feel safe in SOMA, or at least you shouldn't. Each of these things has a particular weakness. You'll never kill one, but this weakness makes it easier to bypass them. They're not hard to figure out, and there aren't many of them to begin with. However, you will spend most of the game dreading what comes next.

That's what SOMA nails. Dreading what comes next. You know the answer before you hear it said out loud, and you still don't want to hear it. But it's impossible to put down. The situation continues to get worse and you can't help but see it to the end. It's Frictional's best game, and a new high standard for horror games.

'SOMA' starts off as a normal day, grounding itself in daily routines & the comfort of the familiar. Before quickly juxtaposing this with the new horror that the protagonist, Simon (sim-1) finds himself in. The game makes fairly large leaps at times leaving the characters emotional reactions to materialise later. For a story that relies deeply upon its characters reflections on their nature and circumstances, these visceral reactions are too often delayed. Simon’s moments of epiphany, which occur three times throughout the game, often occur long after the event. Whether this is because Simon is not the brightest, or that some malfunction from his brain damage causes a delay is not clear. At times Simon’s disengagement from his predicament left me feeling estranged from him in turn, though his later grasping at the tenuous hope that Catherine offers is believable, & the ending a natural consequence of his nebulous emotions. His frail grasp on his newfound reality makes his ultimate fate(s) tragic yet clear when viewed in the wake of Catherine’s insights. The writers deliberately left such things ambiguous, which sadly doesn’t make for a compelling character study. Instead, those characters you do encounter are divested of essential things that make them human, they lack the emotional responses so necessary to elucidate the horror of the situation they find themselves in. Instead, there is a calm, resigned acceptance of their fate.

[h1]"The privilege of being makes a strong case" ~Catherine, in game dialogue[/h1]
At approximately 10-12 hours of play, 'SOMA' doesn’t have much time to work with. Since most of that is spent creeping as stealthily as one can about the environments. The pacing is slow, and with most of the story delivered through objects, diaries, and terminals scattered about the Pathos-II hubs it unfolds in dribs and drabs. This also means that those playing purely for horror and scares won’t find much to appeal. The horror is only apparent once one has truly explored the world, something the game actively hinders when attempting to escape from monsters that disrupt your search.

Hiding and avoiding monsters is the main aspect of play. It’s something established in previous games by Frictional, such as the Amnesia series. Addressing the issue of exploration which is so essential to 'SOMA', a non-death mode was introduced, allowing you to explore freely, which did solve much of the issues around exploration and story.

Exploration is done in the 1st person perspective, which limits your awareness of surroundings. It works brilliantly, not only do you feel embodied when playing from this perspective which of course is important to the ontological themes of the game, but also allows the game to blur your vision at times, dependant on the stress that Simon is experiencing. The perspective is also in a way disorienting, keeping you guessing about Simon’s state. It’s not that other games haven’t used this perspective for good effect before but here the developer’s choice is clear and impactful upon the story itself, leading up to an awareness of yourself-as-Simon that is of pivotal importance in two particular scenes.

[h1]"If we could rebuild even a small part of ourselves, why wouldn't we do that?" ~Catherine[/h1]
The monsters, robotic or humanoid you are avoiding have various ways to navigate past & learning their behaviour is essential to successfully avoid them. Whether looking at them directly, stealthily creeping, or simply running fast to get away, & slamming doors behind you to slow their pursuit. They aren’t particularly frightening or at least aren’t as frightening as you think. It's telling that the game eventually asks what the monster might be, whether it's you (and your decisions), the WAU or the beings themselves. The vague shadowy monsters often distorted your view as they near, or the monstrous ambiguity present in your decisions are what build a cerebral tension. In this, the game plays to its existential themes.

The environment switches between the Atlantic seabed and the industrial interiors Pathos-II itself to create variable stages of calm natural surroundings and the intensity of a decaying complex. Pathos-II is aptly named for the tragedy that plays out within it’s hallways. It’s clear the complex was a height of international, scientific co-operation. From the English and simplified Chinese that dot the terminals and hallways, to the broad cast of characters of multiple nationalities that once inhabited it, to the hope embodied by Catherine and her calm discussions driving you forward. Yet even with this aid, that gives your movement forward impetus, the environments are linear. There is little leeway for exploration other than to find the pieces of story. Only when one is about to encounter a monster does the game shift to a labyrinthine pattern enabling one to dodge & use obstacles to separate oneself from the figures that chase you, quickly changing these segments into games of hide & seek. They do create moments of needed tension, desperately dashing about rooms to uncover as much as possible.
The controls are immensely responsive, and focus purely on movement and observation. Stealth, and running are the two variations on your walking pace, and, as is standard for 1st person, the mouse controls the direction you look, whilst the mouse buttons offer contextualised interactions for solving the various short puzzles that you will encounter. These puzzles are fairly easy to solve, and are varied enough to increase engagement.

The sound design is superb, walking across varied surfaces, will produce different tones, & even walking slower will lower the sound of your footsteps. Venturing out into the water, leads to sounds being distorted, in sharp contrast to the sounds inside Pathos-II. Pathos-II itself creaks and groans, the stress of metal reverberating, as the pressure of water creates new stresses. These clues of your surrounding are alleviated by the comforting sounds of human voices, digitally preserved in various recordings, the emotions lending an analogue feel to the otherwise inhuman situation, & of course Catherine and Simon themselves, Simon’s fluctuating emotions traced with the stress of his situation against Catherine’s non-inflected, rational tones, that emulate her humanity. They are wonderful performances.

SOMA is an ambitious project. With its blend of philosophy and exploration tinged with horror it executes perfectly on its themes. Using a dystopian future lent much needed weight to the story, and expanded on the concept of what a posthumanist position might entail. It is certainly not to the taste of all, but if you are looking for an excellent interpretation of science fiction themes, and solutions for the future that lets you decide for yourself what the negative and positive consequences may be, you will be in good company with SOMA.

~8/10~ Cerebral Transcendence

Soma is beautiful and suberbly crafted , the sheer scale and geometry of some of the underwater structures had me gasping at points. Some of the rusted underwater outpost sections even evoke some of that Stalker sense of discovery. Kind of a mix between Bioshock, Alien isolation and Stalker design wise...but more beautiful.

The game world  itself is huge, highly detailed and reminded me of Half life in several ways, you really do feel like you're in the belly of the beast, just struggling for one tiny glimmer of hope, one shaft of light. it's incredibly oppresive feeling throughout.

I was constantly surprised at the variation and amount of puzzling in the game, I really didn't expect it and went in quite worried that I wouldnt be able to handle the all out horror elements (the tension in Amnesia became unbearable for me).
But the story and it's puzzles were certainly more of the focus. 
There are some very clever sections, that would have had me stumped for months... just like the golden era of pc games.

Thankfully they have a deep and meaningful story to tell (that hit me in the same way as The Swapper) and they want you to experience it and think about it long after.

This game is truly something. I bought it for $4.39 as a cheap scare for a horror night. Instead, I had no idea what I was getting myself into.

The game play is simple. Easy puzzles, straightforward objectives, and a few well-timed scares from the suspense and chase sequences. Honestly, the game play isn’t the reason I’m writing this review at all. It’s serviceable, but it’s not what makes SOMA unforgettable. I only mention it because It's what makes a review valid.

The story is.

SOMA delivers a deep, unsettling, and strangely beautiful reflection on life, identity, and what it actually could mean to exist. I can only say that because I took the time to explore everything: the notes, the recordings, the small details left behind by the crew. I didn’t rush through it like an ordinary player. I let it sit with me.

And that’s where SOMA becomes more than a horror game. The game quietly asks questions about consciousness, morality, and the value of a life that may not even be “real” by our standards. It doesn’t spoon-feed anything, and it doesn’t talk down to the player. Instead, it trusts you to think, to interpret, and to feel the weight.

By the time the credits rolled, I wasn’t scared, or sad (Almost). I was introspective. Uncomfortable. A little shaken. And honestly, grateful that a single game could make me think this much.

For the price I paid, SOMA gave me a perspective on life. If you’re looking for pure horror, you’ll find some. But if you’re open to something deeper, something existential and quietly devastating. SOMA is absolutely worth your time.

After a fatal car crash that killed your girlfriend, you are left with permanent brain damage. Because of the lingering effects of the accident, you agree to an experimental treatment involving a brain scan. And as your brain is scanned, you find yourself in a whole new world, at a site called Upsilon deep underneath the ocean in the year 2104.

SOMA is a first-person survival horror game that throws you into a completely unfamiliar situation and gradually lets you uncover what's going on. But the world you encounter is at the brink of extinction and the technical progress has evolved tremendously, so that it almost takes the entire game to fully understand what's happening.

Since the story is one of the main aspects of the game I'm not going to spoil it. What I can tell you it's smart, very smart. Everything revolves around the question 'what is life?'. And Soma delivers some amazing answers.

The rest of the game is fear, horror, and adventure. The game offers tons of things to explore. You can pick up almost everything. You can read letters, find photos, audio recordings, black boxes, computers, machines, robots, monsters, and many dead and half-dead people.

Soma gets very scary the longer you play. In the beginning, the game is rather tame but the longer you play the scarier it gets. The form of horror is very reminiscent of Alien Isolation. You are chased and have nothing in defense except hiding.

Environmental sounds add a lot to the panic and whenever you turn around you never know who's behind you. Fortunately dying has no severe consequences. Most of the time you restart at the point you died and can continue. Only once did I experience a scene from the other side that I do not want to uncover at this point.

In order to proceed, you often have to solve technical challenges. Find data sources, combine them with the right PC, adjust the PC correctly. There were a few cases in the middle of the game that I found very difficult and could only proceed by searching the internet. I didn't like that but luckily those cases were rare.

In general, the graphics in the game are very nice. But your vision becomes blurry whenever you are attacked. This leads to long stretches where the visuals are not as beautiful as they could be. In my opinion, this degrades the game unnecessarily. You can find specific organic substances growing on surfaces that you can use to heal your vision but there are not too many and using them often lures the monsters on your track.

SOMA is a game in disguise. The star of the game is not the horror and the amazing environment, it's the story. It's one of those stories that keep you brooding about even after finishing the game.

There's a final scene to play after the end credits. In my opinion, this is a very important scene, maybe the most important scene of the game. I'm not sure if it was wise of the developers to hide it behind the credits. [u]If you play the game, please take care not to interrupt the final credits! It makes a difference![/u]

SOMA is a rare kind of game, one that amazes and pulls you in. Made by the creators of such horror classics like Amnesia and Penumbra, SOMA is a psychological horror game where you explore an abandoned underwater facility after earth has been hit by a catastrophe. You look for survivors, make friends and foes and try to save what's left of humanity.

SOMA's greatest strength lies in it's narrative. The questions it asks constantly, about the sense of self and the worth of what it means to be human, are hard-hitting and provide an excellent storyline that keeps you going. The visuals are also excellently done and mesh perfectly with the music and sound. All the 3D artists, level designers and sound engineers deserve a raise. The game looks great and very detailed, has an excellent soundtrack and it all just works well. Dark rooms have eerie music.  When you turn the corner to see the ocean in front of you. the music gets louder and evokes a sense of wonder. It's hard to just write down how great it feels, but you always want to push forward and discover what lies around the corner.

Of course, the game is not without it's flaws. It has some small bugs which can come up, but will most likely not hinder your gameplay experience. Some of the "evade this monster" parts are also a bit annoying. Our main character, Simon, also reacts oddly calmly to most things happening in the game; he only freaks out rarely. He is also a bit ignorant sometimes; it's hard to explain how without spoilers, but it can get a bit irritating.

Overall though, this is an excellent horror walking simulator with some light puzzling and monster evading that will take you about 10-11 hours to play through. It looks excellent, has amazing sound design and a thought-provoking story. It's haunting in all the right ways and a must-play for anyone even remotely into these kind of games.

Personal Rating: 8.5/10.

This is potentially the greatest story rich game ever. A truly spectacular narrative with an even balance of horror, tragedy, ethical dilemmas and philosophical conundrums. The game even forces the player to make impossible choices that don't necessarily effect the story in any drastic way, but leave the player with a sense of unease and dispute about what exactly counts as 'human' and the value of being alive. Whilst the monsters that chase you about the abondoned underwater labs of Pathos II are somewhat alarming, the real horror stems from the psychological torture that the remants of mankind are forced to endure at the hands of their own desire to preserve the ghost of humanity. I think the reason this narrative works so well as a game and not a film is the function of perspective. It's important that the story is percived subjectively to provide context to the plot points and inspire motivation for your decisions. Decent, well fleshed out characters that provoke empathy, even if there are only a few with limited interaction time. And of course the visuals are quite nice as well. Cannot recommend this game enough.
